label: Qubit spectroscopy vs coupler flux
axes: A two-dimensional map: the swept coupler flux bias runs along the horizontal axis, the spectroscopy probe frequency along the vertical axis, and colour encodes the demodulated readout quadrature. The colour scale is auto-ranged per panel, so only contrast against the local background carries meaning. The node draws four overlays on top: one extracted peak-frequency dot per flux column, a polyline joining those extracted points, pale fitted branch curves for the two-level model, and a cross marker at each flux where the fit claims an avoided crossing. A figure may be a single large panel or a row of small panels, one per qubit or per coupled pair, each with its own colour bar.
correct_signature: A single continuous ridge of contrasting colour crosses the map - one dominant frequency per flux column - standing clearly out of the speckled background over most or all of the swept range.

The ridge moves smoothly and gradually: neighbouring flux columns differ by a fraction of a linewidth, so it reads as one connected curve (flat, monotone, or with a single broad turning point) rather than a scatter of disconnected bright cells.
The extracted peak dots lie ON that ridge in essentially every column, and the polyline joining them is as smooth as the ridge itself; dots wandering off into the background are rare and isolated.

When a crossing is claimed, a SECOND feature of visibly different slope approaches the main ridge near the marked flux, the two bend away from each other, and the gap between them narrows to a minimum without the two ever merging - the marker sits at that closest approach.

Both branches stay visible on either side of the claimed crossing, so the bend can be seen to turn around; the feature is bracketed by data rather than running off the end of the sweep or out of the frequency window at the marked flux.
The pale fitted branch curves overlie the bright features they claim to describe, hugging the ridge on both sides of the closest approach and staying roughly symmetric about it.
A claim of NO crossing looks equally correct: one clean, well-tracked, single-branch ridge with no second feature approaching it anywhere in the swept range.

failure_appearance.wrong_peak: The dots latch onto the wrong bright feature - most often a perfectly horizontal stripe holding the same frequency across every flux column (a spurious constant-frequency line, not a flux-tuned qubit), leaving the weaker genuinely flux-dependent ridge untracked; the polyline is then dead straight while the map's real curvature is ignored. A second form: a crossing marker placed where two pale fitted curves intersect each other although no bright feature bends there at all.
failure_appearance.no_signal: Uniform speckle over the whole panel with no ridge anywhere; the extracted dots are sprinkled across the full frequency window with no column-to-column continuity, and the joining polyline zig-zags nearly the full height of the panel between adjacent columns. Observed with a crossing still marked - this family will report a confident crossing on a panel containing no feature whatsoever.
failure_appearance.noisy: The ridge exists over part of the swept flux range and dissolves into speckle over the rest; the dots follow it faithfully where it is visible and scatter randomly where it is not, so the polyline is smooth across one portion and saw-toothed elsewhere. A crossing marker falling in the dissolved portion is unsupported by the picture.
failure_appearance.feature_present_fit_failed: A clear, well-tracked ridge is present and the dots sit on it, yet the pale fitted branch curves sit well away from it - for instance one flat and one gently sloping branch cutting across a region where the actual ridge curves quite differently - so the overlaid model plainly does not describe the visible feature. The claimed crossing then lands where the model's branches meet rather than where the ridge bends.

abstain_when: The colour scale is dominated by a few extreme cells, or the panel is rendered so small, that the ridge cannot be separated from the speckle background at the resolution shown.
The figure holds several panels for different qubits or pairs and nothing in the picture identifies which panel the numeric claim belongs to.
Only a short fragment of the ridge fits inside the frequency window, or it is cut off at a window edge, so a genuine bend cannot be told apart from a straight line.
No marker, overlay or other indication of where the claim sits is drawn, so the claimed location cannot be checked against any feature in the map.
The map is washed out or saturated to a near-uniform colour with only the overlays legible - overlays alone are never evidence, since they are drawn whether or not a feature exists.
notes:
The premise supplied with this task was wrong in two ways and a maintainer must know both. (1) The single figure named as node-accepted belongs to a run whose own stored fit result records failure with zero crossings - it is not an acceptance and must not be used as this family's positive exemplar. (2) Negative runs ARE archived for this family, in quantity: across the archived corpus roughly three quarters of per-target fits report zero crossings. Every failure appearance above was therefore read off real archived panels rather than invented. Only drifted is left null - nothing resembling a ridge migrating out of the frequency window or a run-to-run drift was seen, and since this node sweeps flux rather than time, drift may not be expressible here at all.

Twelve panels were examined across two independent archives and two node generations: older single-target sweeps over a wide flux range, rendered large and very noisy, and newer narrow-range multi-panel per-pair tiles with much cleaner ridges. The two styles look so different that the judge must not calibrate its notion of sufficient contrast on either one alone.

The most important lesson: this family's fitter false-accepts. Among the panels flagged successful, several put the claimed closest approach at the very edge of the swept flux range, with data on only one side of it and no visible second branch anywhere; at least one flags a crossing on a panel that is pure speckle with no ridge at all. A judge that merely confirms a marker was drawn will pass all of those. Require the bend itself - two features of differing slope, repelling, bracketed by data on both sides.

The converse trap is just as common: a clean, well-tracked single ridge reported as zero crossings is a CORRECT result, not a failure. Absence of a crossing is the usual honest outcome for this node, so no marker must never by itself be read as a bad figure.

Overlay semantics are not labelled anywhere in the figure, so they are recorded here: per-column extracted peak dots, a polyline joining them, pale two-branch model curves, and a cross at each claimed crossing. Their presence proves nothing; only their agreement with the bright ridge does. Colour bars are auto-ranged per panel, so absolute colour values and the numbers printed beside the colour bar carry no cross-run meaning - judge contrast against the local background only.

localizer is none: although the claimed quantity is a position along the flux axis and could in principle be pointed at, confirming it requires reading the whole plane - the second branch, the repulsion gap, and the ridge curvature on both sides - so this entry is signature-trust-only rather than crop-and-point.
